title: Have / had / had
subtitle: have breakfast, have a look, have got
summary: Use have with meals, lessons and drinks, learn the everyday expressions with have, and use have got and have to.

lesson.heading: What can you have?
lesson.text: **Have** goes with a lot of everyday words. You can **have** a meal, **have** a party, **have** a lesson or **have** a drink. Learn the words in groups - it is much easier to remember them.

examples.text: I always **have** coffee in the morning.
We can **have** dinner before the film, or we can eat after it.
I **have** an exam tomorrow, so I have to study tonight.

lesson.heading: have + these words
rows: a party / a meeting / a game (of football, tennis ...)
a cup of tea / a cup of coffee / a drink / an ice cream / some cheese
a shower / a bath / a swim

lesson.heading: Expressions with have
lesson.text: These expressions are very common. **Have a look** means look at it. **Have a go** means try it or ride it. **Have a word with someone** means speak to them. **Have a good time** means enjoy yourself.

examples.text: Is that your camera? Can I **have a look**?
Is that your bicycle? Can I **have a go**?
Do you **have a moment**? Can I **have a word** with you?
We always **have a good time** in our English lessons.

lesson.heading: have my hair cut / have the time
lesson.text: When someone else does something for you, we say **have something done**. And if you are too busy for something, you say you do not **have the time**.

examples.text: I'm going to **have my hair cut**. Can you meet me at the hairdresser's?
I want to learn to ski but I don't **have the time**.

left.label: have got (speaking / informal)
left.text: We use have got a lot when we speak.
examples: It's **got** five bedrooms and three bathrooms.
I've **got** a cold. / I've **got** a headache.

right.label: have (writing / formal)
right.text: We use have on its own in writing.
examples: Do you **have** any brothers and sisters?
*A:* Do you sell postcards? *B:* Yes, but we **haven't got** any at the moment.

lesson.heading: have to / have got to
lesson.text: We use **have to** or **have got to** when the situation means you must do something. In the past we use **had to**, without *got*.

examples.text: The museum's not free. You **have to** pay $10 to go in.
All students **have to** do an exam.
My sister needs the car, so I've **got to** walk to school this week.
When I was a student, I **had to** write an essay every week.

lesson.text: Group expressions that belong to the same topic: have + meals (breakfast, lunch, dinner), have + study words (a lesson, an exam, homework).

exercises.prompt: I have a tennis ___ every Saturday morning. My teacher is excellent.
exercises.explanation: We have a lesson, an exam or homework.

exercises.prompt: Evelyn's having a ___ on Saturday. All her friends are invited. Are you going?
exercises.explanation: We have a party, a meeting or a game.

exercises.prompt: I have an ___ tomorrow, so I have to study tonight.
exercises.explanation: We have an exam or a test.

exercises.prompt: Is that your bicycle? Can I have a ___? I'd love to ride it.
exercises.explanation: Have a go means try it or ride it.

exercises.prompt: Is that your new camera? Can I have a ___?
exercises.explanation: Have a look means look at it.

exercises.prompt: What do you say in each situation? Match them.

pairs.left: Someone is going away on a long trip.
Someone sneezes and has a red nose.
Your friend has a new camera.
You need to speak to your teacher.
pairs.right: Can I have a word with you?

pairs.left: Your friend has a new bicycle.

exercises.statement: Scarlett has gone to the hairdresser's to have cut her hair.
exercises.explanation: Scarlett has gone to the hairdresser's to have her hair cut.

exercises.statement: I want to have some words with my teacher after the lesson.
exercises.explanation: I want to have a word with my teacher after the lesson.

exercises.prompt: Mum didn't have the ___ to go to the shop today. She was too busy.
exercises.explanation: We say I don't have the time, not the times.

exercises.prompt: We say have + all of these. Put each one in the right group.
Everybody at the school must do this test. Say it.
exercises.answer: All students have to do an exam.
exercises.explanation: Have to means the situation makes you do it.

exercises.prompt: When I was a student, I ___ write an essay every week.
exercises.explanation: In the past we say had to, without got.

exercises.statement: They don't have any cake in the cafe today.
exercises.explanation: Correct. You can also say: They haven't got any cake today.
